video_title: Lawfare Daily: Can State Laws Protect Against Misuse of the National Guard?
gist: Brennan Center researchers Liza and Joseph, joined by Lawfare senior editor Lauren Voss, discuss their new 50-state compendium of National Guard law, concluding that Title 32/Section 502F deployments (currently active in DC, Tennessee, and Louisiana) evade the federal Posse Comitatus Act because no state has an equivalent statute, that several states have unconstitutional martial-law and mass-arrest statutes still on the books, and that Virginia's new oversight law offers the clearest template for state legislatures to reassert control.

themes.theme: The Legal Architecture of National Guard Deployment

insights.claim: The National Guard operates under three distinct statuses: state active duty (governed by state law, commanded by the governor), Title 10 (federalized, commanded by the president, same status as active-duty military), and Title 32 — a hybrid status where the Guard nominally remains under gubernatorial command while performing a federally funded mission.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editor
insights.so_what: This three-tier framework is the baseline for assessing legal risk in any domestic Guard deployment; investors/analysts tracking political and regulatory risk should identify which status applies before assuming Posse Comitatus protections exist.

insights.claim: Section 502F of Title 32 (specifically the 2006-added subsection 502F(2)(A)) allows a governor to deploy the National Guard to support a federal mission at the request of the president or Secretary of Defense, with almost no statutory text defining the scope of what missions qualify.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: The vagueness of 502F's text is the specific legal hinge enabling expansive domestic use of the Guard; any future deployment justified under 502F should be scrutinized against its narrow legislative history (disaster response, counter-drug support) rather than its broad literal wording.

insights.claim: Legislative history indicates Congress designed 502F to fund the Guard's traditional disaster-response and counter-drug functions, not to authorize suppression of civil unrest or general crime control, yet the Trump administration has used it for exactly those purposes — starting with 2020 protest deployments (11 states sent Guard to DC after George Floyd's killing) and now for 'crime control' missions in DC, Memphis, and New Orleans.
insights.speaker: Liza, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Establishes a repeatable precedent: an administration can invoke 502F for domestic policing missions well outside its original intent, which is a template likely to recur in future administrations regardless of party.

insights.claim: Nearly 5,000 National Guard troops are currently deployed in Washington DC, largely standing idle rather than performing substantive law-enforcement tasks, and President Trump has said the deployment will continue until January 2029 — an open-ended, effectively permanent posture rather than the traditional short-term crisis response.
insights.speaker: Liza, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Signals a durable shift from emergency-response use of the military to a standing, quasi-permanent domestic military presence — a structural change in US domestic governance with implications for civil-liberties and municipal-cost analysis.

insights.claim: Although Title 32 nominally leaves 'command and control' with the governor, in practice only administrative (paperwork) control stays with the state in the DC deployment — both tactical control (people on the ground) and operational control (mission definition, priorities) run through the DC National Guard and a federal joint task force chain.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editor
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that the legal fiction of 'state control' under Title 32 does not match operational reality, undermining any assumption that gubernatorial command meaningfully constrains federal use of deployed Guard forces.

themes.theme: The Posse Comitatus Gap at the State Level

insights.claim: No US state or territory has a law equivalent to the federal Posse Comitatus Act, which is a 'clear statement rule' requiring express legislative authorization (not case-by-case approval) before the president can use the military for law enforcement — a gap the Brennan Center's nationwide compendium confirmed is universal.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: The single most important finding of the compendium: without a state-level equivalent, Title 32 deployments face essentially no analogous federal-style check, making state legislative reform the primary available remedy.
insights.quote: There is no state that has a law saying that a governor's deployment of the National Guard for law enforcement has to be pursuant to an express statutory authorization.

insights.claim: The Posse Comitatus Act applies only to federal officials and federalized (Title 10) forces, not to state officials or Title 32 National Guard, which is precisely why Title 32/502F has become the preferred legal vehicle for domestic military deployment under this administration.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific statutory loophole being exploited, useful for anticipating that any future administration seeking to expand domestic military use will similarly route through Title 32 rather than Title 10.

insights.claim: The historical absence of state-level Posse Comitatus equivalents partly reflects that most state Guard statutes and constitutional provisions predate a major shift in the National Guard's role: since the end of the draft, and especially since the late 1990s and post-9/11, the Guard has been increasingly integrated into combat deployments, with roughly half of Iraq/Afghanistan troops drawn from the Guard/Reserve versus under 1% in Vietnam, and over one million Guard members having done combat tours.
insights.speaker: Liza, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Undercuts the traditional assumption that the Guard is less suited to combat-style domestic policing than active-duty forces — today's Guard increasingly shares the same training and 'battle mindset' as active duty, raising the stakes of using it domestically without Posse-Comitatus-style constraints.

insights.claim: An Illinois statute (20 Illinois Compiled Statutes) purports to allow the National Guard, when deployed in response to civil unrest, to arrest any person in view without process and detain them indefinitely — a provision Joseph calls unconstitutional on its face under the Fourth, Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments and the right to habeas corpus, yet it remains on the books.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: A live, unrepealed statute that could be invoked in a crisis despite being unenforceable — a concrete legal-risk flag for anyone tracking Illinois emergency-powers exposure.

insights.claim: Iowa Code section 29A.46 purports to let the governor set up military tribunals to try civilians in areas placed under martial law, which Joseph says conflicts with the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments and with Supreme Court precedent (Ex parte Milligan, Duncan v. Kahanamoku) holding that even where martial law is otherwise permissible, military trial of civilians is not — and it also conflicts with Iowa's own state constitution.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Another concrete, currently-live unconstitutional statute; both the Iowa and Illinois examples show state legislatures have not cleaned up facially unconstitutional emergency-powers law even decades after enactment.

insights.claim: Thirteen states have a statutory-constitutional conflict where the state constitution requires the military be subordinate to civil power, yet a state statute purports to authorize the governor to declare martial law; Tennessee is the starkest example — its constitution explicitly prohibits declaring 'martial rule,' yet a Tennessee statute purports to authorize exactly that.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable list (13 states) of jurisdictions where martial-law statutes are legally void on their face — useful for any legal-risk assessment of a hypothetical martial-law declaration in those states.

insights.claim: No state governor has declared martial law since the governor of Maryland did so in 1963, but many states still retain martial-law-authorizing statutes enacted mostly during the 1861-1945 period — dormant but legally live.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Establishes a long dormancy period that could create false confidence; these statutes remain available tools for a governor willing to test them despite eight decades of disuse.

insights.claim: State law on National Guard 'peace officer' status (the authority to make arrests) varies enormously: Missouri and Arkansas make every Guard member a peace officer by default whenever on duty regardless of law-enforcement training, while other states restrict peace-officer status only to trained military police.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration of how uneven state-by-state legal exposure is for Guard members and the public they interact with, relevant to assessing liability and due-process risk by state.

insights.claim: Many states' National Guard laws (Wisconsin and New York are cited examples) are simply vague or underdeveloped, lacking clear deployment criteria, which leaves broad discretion to the governor by default rather than by deliberate design.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Identifies a first-order reform priority: even before addressing law-enforcement powers, many states need basic statutory clarity on when a governor may deploy the Guard at all.

themes.theme: Reform: Virginia's Model and the Path Forward

insights.claim: The Brennan Center's core reform recommendation is for states to enact their own 'mini Posse Comitatus Acts' that flip the default from broad gubernatorial discretion to requiring the Guard be used for law enforcement only pursuant to specific statutes enacted by the state legislature — not a ban on Guard law-enforcement use, but a requirement that legislatures, not governors alone, define its scope.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable legislative template that state lawmakers in any state could adopt now, giving a concrete benchmark for grading future state legislative sessions on Guard oversight.

insights.claim: Virginia's recently enacted HB86 is held up as a partial model: it requires the Adjutant General to submit an annual report on the Virginia Guard's status, federal funding, and use by federal authorities; it slightly narrows the governor's deployment authority; it reinforces existing prohibitions on using the Guard for election interference; and it creates a working group to study further reforms.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-passed legislative template other states can copy verbatim or adapt, making it the most immediately trackable benchmark for state-level Guard oversight reform.

insights.claim: Tennessee is one of the few states where existing state law actually constrained a Guard deployment: a lower court found the Memphis Guard deployment violated Tennessee's own statutory limits, though that ruling is currently stayed pending appeal.
insights.speaker: Liza, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Proof-of-concept that state law can function as a real check where it exists and is specific enough — a live case to monitor as a bellwether for whether state courts will enforce these limits against a federally directed mission.

insights.claim: The primary federal restriction on troops at polling places, 18 U.S.C. 592, bars both the military and 'federal civil officers' from polling sites — meaning that even a Title 32 deployment nominally under gubernatorial command could still trigger liability under 592 if the president or Secretary of Defense directed it as a federal mission.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editor
insights.so_what: Clarifies that the 'state command' framing does not necessarily shield a Title 32 deployment from election-related legal exposure, an important nuance for assessing 2026 midterm deployment risk.

insights.claim: Separate from 592, both state and federal voter-intimidation laws apply to anyone regardless of deployment authority or intent, depend only on effect (not intent), and — unlike 592 — can be enforced through private lawsuits, making them the more practical backstop against Guard involvement in intimidating voters.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Identifies the most enforceable legal remedy available if Guard forces are used near polling places in 2026, relevant for anyone assessing election-integrity risk.

insights.claim: Both guests describe a severe, current lack of public transparency about which legal authority (Title 10, Title 32, or state active duty) governs any given National Guard deployment and what its mission scope actually is, making real-time legal or legislative oversight extremely difficult.
insights.speaker: Liza, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural information gap that itself is a policy target — greater mandatory disclosure of deployment legal authority and mission scope (as Virginia's law begins to require) would materially improve accountability.

insights.claim: Guard members deployed on open-ended domestic missions are pulled away both from their civilian jobs (teachers, healthcare workers, shopkeepers) and from the military training and readiness they would otherwise be doing for foreign-threat response, a hidden cost to both their home communities and national defense readiness.
insights.speaker: Joseph, Brennan Center
insights.so_what: A second-order cost of prolonged domestic deployments — lost military readiness and community labor capacity — that is rarely counted in the public debate over these deployments' benefits.

insights.claim: Guard members are generally not well trained in the legal distinctions between arrest and detention, creating downstream due-process complications for anyone they detain — illustrated by a specific example of a Guard detention near the Dupont Circle Metro station in DC.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editor
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration of practical legal risk (weak criminal cases, civil-liability exposure) created by using undertrained military personnel for law-enforcement-adjacent tasks.
